name: FastAPI
summary: A Python API framework built on Starlette and Pydantic: declare parameters and models with type hints, and it validates requests, serializes responses and generates an OpenAPI document with interactive docs.
intro: FastAPI is Starlette with an API layer on top. The `FastAPI` class subclasses `Starlette`, so routing, middleware, WebSockets and the ASGI interface are Starlette’s, and an ASGI server such as Uvicorn runs it. What FastAPI adds is reading your function signatures. A path operation is a function under a decorator such as `@app.get("/items/{item_id}")`, and its parameters say where each value comes from (path, query string, header, cookie, or a JSON body declared as a Pydantic model) and what type it must be. FastAPI reads the body as JSON, converts and validates every value with Pydantic, and answers `422` with the location of each error before your function runs. The return value passes through the declared return type or `response_model`, which validates it and filters out any field the model doesn’t list. The same declarations become an OpenAPI document with a JSON Schema for every model, served as Swagger UI at `/docs` and ReDoc at `/redoc`.

Dependencies are plain functions passed to `Depends()`. FastAPI calls them before the endpoint and injects their results, and dependencies can have dependencies of their own; that is how authentication, database sessions and shared parameters are wired. Endpoints and dependencies can be `async def`, which run on the event loop, or plain `def`, which FastAPI runs in a thread pool so they don’t block the server. GraphQL libraries plug in through ASGI. The docs recommend Strawberry, whose `GraphQLRouter` is a FastAPI router, so REST and GraphQL endpoints share one app and the same dependencies. FastAPI is still at 0.x (0.143.0 came out on October 8, 2026), and its docs say a new minor version may contain breaking changes, so pin the version you use.
strengths: One type declaration gives parsing, conversion, validation, editor completion and API docs, with no separate schema language to keep in step
OpenAPI and JSON Schema generated from the code, with Swagger UI and ReDoc built in and client generators able to read the same document
Dependency injection with sub-dependencies and no registration step, used for auth, database sessions and GraphQL context alike
Everything Starlette has (WebSockets, background tasks, mounts, a test client), and any ASGI library, such as a GraphQL server, can sit beside your routes
limits: Still 0.x after nearly eight years: minor releases may break things, so pin the version and read the release notes before upgrading
Tied to Pydantic: moving to Pydantic 2 needed model changes, and 0.126.0 (December 2025) dropped Pydantic 1 support
Plain `def` endpoints and dependencies share Starlette’s thread pool, 40 threads by default; blocking I/O inside `async def` holds up every request on that worker
No database layer, admin or migrations of its own: the SQL tutorial brings in SQLModel, which is built on SQLAlchemy and Pydantic
Validation and serialization cost CPU on every request, and FastAPI can’t be faster than the Starlette layer it runs on

snippet.title: A path operation with a dependency and a response model
source: # pip install fastapi httpx2   (serve it for real with: fastapi dev main.py)
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, Header, HTTPException
def current_user(x_token: Annotated[str, Header()]) -> str:  # a dependency
async def read_item(item_id: int, user: Annotated[str, Depends(current_user)]):
return ITEMS[item_id]  # supplier_cost is filtered out by ItemOut

sections.title: GraphQL beside REST: FastAPI, Strawberry and SQLAlchemy
sections.intro: The stack from the Python GraphQL API architecture, small enough to run. FastAPI routes `/graphql` to Strawberry’s router, Strawberry hands the query to graphql-core, and the resolver loads rows through an async SQLAlchemy session that a FastAPI dependency opens per request. SQLite stands in for PostgreSQL so it runs anywhere; only the engine URL changes.
source: # In production the URL is PostgreSQL, e.g. "postgresql+asyncpg://app@db/shop".
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column
class Order:  # Strawberry: a GraphQL type
async def orders(self, info: strawberry.Info, customer: str) -> list[Order]:
return [Order(id=r.id, total_cents=r.total_cents) for r in rows]
async def get_context():  # a FastAPI dependency: one session per request
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):  # create and fill the table at startup
@app.get("/health")  # ordinary REST routes sit beside it
# 200 Argument 'Query.orders(customer:)' of type 'String!' is required, but it was not provided.

story: Sebastián Ramírez had spent several years building APIs for machine learning and distributed systems and leading the teams behind them. Ramírez’s favourite stack was Flask with Flask-apispec, Marshmallow and Webargs, and Ramírez built full-stack project generators on it. But the schemas were Marshmallow classes rather than Python types, and with plug-ins such as APISpec the API description was YAML in docstrings, which went stale whenever someone changed the code and forgot the YAML. The closest thing to what Ramírez wanted was APIStar, which declared parameters with type hints and generated OpenAPI, until its creator turned to Starlette and APIStar stopped being a web framework.

Before writing FastAPI, Ramírez spent several months studying the OpenAPI, JSON Schema and OAuth2 specifications, and tried out API designs in PyCharm, VS Code and Jedi-based editors. Ramírez picked Pydantic for data and Starlette for the web layer and contributed to both, including making Pydantic fully compliant with JSON Schema. FastAPI 0.1.0 was published on December 8, 2018, and its docs call it a “spiritual successor” to APIStar.

Because FastAPI hands all data work to Pydantic, Pydantic’s rewrite shaped it. FastAPI 0.100.0 (July 2023) supported Pydantic 2, whose core is written in Rust, while keeping Pydantic 1 working, and 0.126.0 (December 2025) dropped Pydantic 1. In 2026 it moved to Python 3.10 or later, added support for Starlette 1.0 in 0.133.0, and gained native OpenTelemetry support in 0.142.0, still under a 0.x version number.

choices.choice: Build on Starlette and Pydantic instead of from scratch
choices.why: Starlette already had the routing, WebSockets and speed, but no validation, serialization or docs; Pydantic did validation and JSON Schema from type hints. FastAPI only adds the layer that joins them, and the `FastAPI` class subclasses `Starlette`.

choices.choice: Standard Python type hints, not a custom schema language
choices.why: APISpec’s YAML docstrings were a second language inside Python strings that editors couldn’t help with. Plain type hints give completion and type checks, and the design was tested in the editors that, by the Python Developer Survey, about 80% of Python developers use.

choices.choice: Open standards for the API description
choices.why: Hug generated its own JSON description of an API, not OpenAPI, so tools such as Swagger UI couldn’t easily use it. FastAPI emits OpenAPI and JSON Schema, so standard docs UIs and client generators work with it.

The dependency injection in NestJS, APIStar and Molten needed components registered up front. In FastAPI a dependency is a function named in a parameter’s `Depends()`, so there is nothing to register.
